PARA.TITLE: Outline of In-vehicle Multiplex Communication System

ITEM.PTXT: As in-vehicle multiplex communication systems intended to simplify the vehicle wire harness and speed up communication, 3 types have been adopted: CAN (Controller Area Network) communication enabling high-speed communication, LIN (Local Interconnect Network) communication enabling low-cost multiplex communication, and AVC-LAN (Audio Visual Communication-Local Area Network) communication for the audio system.

By connecting the diagnostic tool "TaSCAN" to the vehicle side connector (DLC3: Data Link Connector No.3), each ECU can be accessed via the gateway computer and the various multiplex communication lines. This allows output of DTCs, data monitoring (checking ECU data, etc.), Active Test (driving actuators as desired), customization (setting control programs), etc. For details, refer to the Repair Manual.

A CAN [ISO11898] communication system has been adopted, which transmits multiple items of information and data converted into digital signals by the communication circuit over a pair of communication lines (twisted pair wiring). This reduces the wire harness and streamlines the electronic control systems connecting the input systems (sensors, switches, etc.), control units and output systems (motors, etc.).
CAN is an abbreviation for Controller Area Network, a serial communication conforming to ISO (International Organization for Standardization) standards.

The CAN communication system uses 2 communication lines (bus), CAN High and CAN Low, as a pair, determines the bus level from their differential voltage, and transmits it as a digital signal conforming to a dedicated communication protocol (communication rules) at a speed of 500kbps (V bus) or 250kbps (MS bus).
There are dominant and recessive bus levels; in the CAN communication system, dominant is logically judged as "0" and recessive as "1".
A unit expressing signal transmission speed. "500kbps" indicates that 500000 bits of data are transmitted in 1 second(s).

By dividing the CAN communication main line into 2 systems (V bus system/MS bus system) via the meter ECU, the communication load within the CAN communication bus due to the increased number of connected computers has been reduced.

The CAN communication system is configured as a bus type network in which multiple computers are connected to 2 common communication lines; the CAN communication lines used as the main lines (common communication lines) are V bus No.1 (communication speed 500kbs) from the meter ECU to the engine control ECU, V bus No.2 (communication speed 500kbs) from the CAN gateway computer to junction connector No.4, and the MS bus (communication speed 250kbs) from the meter ECU to the Main Body ECU.
Terminating resistors (120 Ω) are provided on the bus main line. This allows the differential voltage to be determined from the loop-connected network.

The CAN communication system is a time-division multiplex bidirectional communication system in which all computers (ECUs) and sensors that make up the network can both transmit and receive data at staggered times using a pair of communication lines (bus). Therefore, each ECU and sensor communicates in accordance with a common communication protocol (communication rules) so that communication is performed smoothly and reliably.

The CAN communication protocol adopts the CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) method as the rule for sending data to the communication lines, so that all ECUs and sensors can share a pair of communication lines while each has the right to start transmitting data.

Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: communication access control in which each ECU constantly senses the state of the communication line (carrier) and starts transmitting data only when no other data is flowing on the line. In addition, control in which, when a data collision (data transmitted simultaneously from another ECU) is detected, data is transmitted again after waiting for a fixed period of time.

Each ECU and sensor starts transmitting data when no other data is flowing on the CAN bus; when 2 or more ECUs or sensors start transmitting at the same time, the system determines the transmission priority according to the ID information contained in the transmitted data itself.
The data used in the CAN communication system consists of a frame made up of "ID", "DLC", "DATA", "CRC", "ACK", etc.

To reduce the communication load between ECUs caused by the increase in ECUs in the CAN communication circuit due to increased functionality, a CAN gateway computer has been adopted and the CAN communication main line has been divided into 2 systems.
Highly important data from each ECU is set as a priority frame with a short delay time, reducing the data transmission delay within the gateway.
When the CAN gateway computer detects a malfunction in itself, it stops relaying data between buses to avoid transmitting incorrect data.
LIN communication (LIN: Local Interconnect Network) has been adopted on all models.

LIN communication is used for sending and receiving security signals between the certification ECU and the main body ECU, steering lock ECU, ID code box, etc., and for sending and receiving air conditioning signals between the air conditioning control panel and air conditioning ECU.

Multiplex communication is a system in which multiple ECUs are connected to 1 communication line and can exchange data with each other. This makes it possible to suppress the increase in wiring when systems are integrated or functions are added.
LIN communication uses a single communication wire and transmits digital signals conforming to a dedicated communication protocol (communication rules) at a speed of 20kbps.

It is equipped with a diagnosis function that informs the technician of system malfunctions and a fail-safe function that ensures minimum performance of each ECU and protects the system when a communication malfunction occurs between ECUs.
A single-master method is adopted, in which the main body ECU controls sleep (low current mode), wake-up (standby mode), etc. of the ECUs it communicates with.
LIN communication is a multiplex communication network intended mainly for data communication between body control ECUs.

ITEM.PTXT: The LIN communication system is a time-division multiplex bidirectional communication system in which all ECUs making up the network use 1 communication line, sending data by staggering the timing at which each ECU uses the communication line while also being able to receive. For this reason, each ECU communicates according to a common communication protocol (communication rules) so that communication is performed smoothly and reliably.
Data used in the LIN communication system consists of digital signals containing information such as the identification ID of each ECU (node ID) and the communication data contents.

As the communication rule for sending onto the communication line, so that all ECUs can share 1 communication line based on a defined transmission schedule, a single-master method is adopted in which the main body ECU controls the communication timing, sleep (low current mode), wake-up (standby mode), etc. of the ECUs it communicates with.
